title: How Does Your Screen Make Every Color?
sources: MyTutor / The Naked Scientists 'drop magnifier': a small water droplet on a screen acts as a magnifying lens, so you can see the individual red, green and blue sub-pixels
Electronics360 'How your computer actually creates color': each pixel is made of red, green and blue sub-pixels whose brightness is varied to make colours (additive RGB)
TechTerms 'Color depth' / Harvard CSCI E-12: 8 bits per channel = 256 levels each for red, green and blue; 256 x 256 x 256 = 16,777,216 (about 16.7 million) colours
Additive colour mixing (Hanover College ISLE, EIU physics notes): red + green + blue at full = white, all off = black, red + green light = yellow
Eye/brain: sub-pixels are too small to resolve at normal viewing distance, so the eye's cones blend neighbouring red and green light and we perceive yellow

lines.text: How does your screen make every single color you see?
lines.caps: HOW DOES YOUR *SCREEN | MAKE EVERY *SINGLE | *COLOR YOU SEE?

lines.text: Well, put a drop of water on it, and look closely.
lines.caps: WELL PUT A *DROP | OF *WATER ON IT | AND LOOK *CLOSELY

lines.text: Every pixel is really three tiny lights,
one red, one green and one blue.
Each light can glow at two hundred and fifty six brightness levels,
and mixing them gives over sixteen million colors.
All three at full blast? That's white.
the yellow in these captions isn't yellow light at all.
lines.caps: THE *YELLOW | IN THESE *CAPTIONS | ISN'T YELLOW *LIGHT | AT *ALL

lines.text: It's just red and green, glowing side by side,
lines.caps: IT'S JUST *RED | AND *GREEN | GLOWING *SIDE BY SIDE

lines.text: and your brain blends them into yellow.
Three tiny lights, and your eyes do the rest.
lines.caps: THREE TINY *LIGHTS | AND YOUR *EYES | DO THE *REST
